questions: Which propagation method separates an established clump into several plants, each with roots and shoots?
Division splits a rooted clump; the alternatives do not divide it into rooted plants.
A piece of a plant grown into a new plant
A fruit removed before it ripens
Cuttings use vegetative pieces; seeds, harvested fruit and preserved flowers are distinct.
When grafting a rose, what does the rootstock supply?
The colour of every petal directly
The rootstock is the rooted partner; scion growth forms the selected flowering variety.
What is micropropagation used to produce?
New plants from tiny pieces of plant tissue
Micropropagation cultures plant tissue; none of the alternatives grows plants this way.
During propagation by layering, when is a shoot normally detached from its parent?
After it has formed its own roots
Before it is bent towards the soil
As soon as its first flower opens
Layering roots an attached stem, unlike a cutting detached before rooting.
What does a gardener do when 'hardening off' seedlings?
Gradually gets them used to outdoor conditions
Presses their compost into a solid block
Dries them until their leaves become brittle
Hardening off acclimatises indoor-raised plants; physical hardening and drying are not the process.
Does hardening off make a frost-sensitive plant fully frost-hardy?
No; it can still be damaged by frost
Yes; it prevents all freezing damage
Yes; but only if the leaves turn yellow
Only if all the flowers are removed
Acclimatisation does not remove a tender plant's intrinsic frost sensitivity.
Why are crowded seedlings thinned out?
To reduce competition for space and resources
To prevent every remaining plant from flowering
To turn annual plants into perennials
To stop roots from taking up water
Thinning reduces crowding; it does not change life cycle or block root uptake.
When lifting a delicate seedling to transplant it, which part is safest to hold gently?
A leaf can be replaced more readily than a crushed stem or damaged growth point.
What does 'pricking out' mean when raising seedlings?
Moving individual seedlings into more space
Piercing every seed with a fork
Removing the flower buds from a mature shrub
Scratching the bark of a tree
Pricking out is individual seedling transplantation, not puncturing plant tissues.
What is a seed drill in a garden bed?
A shallow groove made for sowing seeds
A device for drilling into tree trunks
A hole made by a feeding caterpillar
A container for storing dried flowers
Here drill means the sowing groove rather than a powered tool.
A seed packet says 'sow direct'. What should you do?
Sow where the plants are intended to grow
Grow every seed in water first
Remove the seed coats before planting
Keep the seeds in darkness permanently
Direct sowing avoids the initial container-and-transplant stage.
Which soil type usually feels gritty and allows water to drain through quickly?
Grit and rapid drainage together identify sand; other listed types have different textures or retention.
Which garden soil is typically sticky when wet and can bake hard in dry weather?
Clay's fine particles give the stated wet and dry behaviour.
Which soil description means a mixture of sand, silt and clay?
Loam combines the three mineral particle classes; peat is mainly organic.
Which plant is a good example of an acid-loving garden shrub?
Rhododendrons are ericaceous; the listed Mediterranean herbs and lilac do not share this acid-soil requirement.
What does the pH of garden soil describe?
pH measures acidity, not depth, animal population or temperature.
Where is a mulch normally placed around garden plants?
On the surface of the soil
Across the top of every leaf
Under the drainage holes of a pot
Mulch is a surface covering, unlike leaf coatings or pot drainage material.
Which is a useful effect of an organic mulch around plants?
Preventing all rainfall from entering the soil
Replacing the plant's need for sunlight
Mulch conserves soil moisture; it does not eliminate water entry or photosynthesis.
Which of these can slowly decompose when used as garden mulch?
Bark is organic and biodegradable; the three mineral or glass alternatives are not.
Which part of a flowering plant is removed during deadheading?
Deadheading removes spent blooms, not healthy vegetative parts.
Why might a gardener leave some faded flowers on a plant instead of deadheading them?
To allow seed heads to develop
To stop the roots from absorbing minerals
To change the species of the plant
To make all its leaves evergreen
Leaving spent flowers permits seed development; the alternatives are unrelated.
For many repeat-flowering plants, deadheading can encourage what?
A change from leaves to needles
Removing spent flowers can support further flowering but does not change basic plant form.
Which of these garden plants grows from a true bulb?
Tulips have true bulbs; gladioli have corms, bearded irises rhizomes and dahlias tuberous roots.
What type of underground storage organ does a gladiolus have?
Gladiolus is a corm-bearing plant; its storage organ is not a layered true bulb.
Which spring-flowering plant grows from a corm?
Crocus has a corm; the other three examples have true bulbs.
What distinguishes a true bulb from a corm when cut open?
A true bulb has fleshy layers; a corm is solid inside
A true bulb contains no living tissue
A corm is always hollow inside
A true bulb has a woody trunk inside
True bulbs store food in fleshy scale leaves; corms are solid swollen stems.
A rhizome is best described as which type of plant structure?
A horizontal stem that can produce roots and shoots
Rhizomes are modified stems, not reproductive cells or coverings.
In a typical UK garden, when are most spring-flowering bulbs planted?
Only after their spring flowers open
In midsummer after removing all roots
Autumn planting precedes the usual spring display; the prompt fixes the climate context.
When planting a tulip bulb, which way should its pointed growing tip usually face?
It must be cut off first
The growing tip goes upwards; the basal plate and roots sit below.
Daffodils belong to which botanical genus?
Narcissus is the daffodil genus; each distractor is a separate familiar flower genus.
Which feature gives a typical daffodil flower its familiar trumpet-like centre?
The central corona forms the cup or trumpet; the other structures are outside the flower display.
Which botanical name identifies the snowdrop genus?
Galanthus is snowdrop; the similar-sounding genera name different flowering plants.
What colour are the flowers of the common snowdrop, Galanthus nivalis?
Common snowdrops have white segments with green markings on the inner ones.
Which spot is generally suitable for snowdrops in a garden?
A hot, dry sand bed in full sun
Snowdrops suit partial shade and avoid permanent waterlogging and excessive summer drought.
Which growing conditions generally suit lavender best?
An unlit room and wet compost
Lavender is a sun-loving plant that dislikes wet soil and shade.
Lavandula is the botanical genus of which aromatic plant?
Lavandula identifies lavender; the other aromatic herbs belong to different genera.
Which garden plant is known for fragrant flower spikes above grey-green foliage?
The combination of aromatic spikes and grey-green foliage distinguishes lavender among these options.
What is the usual growth habit of a wisteria?
Wisteria climbs with twining woody branches; the other habits do not apply.
What is the botanical term for the long hanging flower clusters of wisteria?
Racemes are flower clusters; the alternatives are stems, seed leaves or storage organs.
Which structures help climbing sweet peas cling to supports?
Sweet pea tendrils coil onto supports; the other structures are not its climbing mechanism.
What is the botanical name of the fragrant annual sweet pea?
Lathyrus odoratus is ornamental annual sweet pea; the distractors are food legumes.
Why does regularly picking sweet pea flowers often prolong flowering?
It reduces the plant's investment in developing seed pods
It permanently prevents roots from growing
It changes the flowers into perennial stems
Picking blooms before pod formation encourages more flowers; the alternatives are false.
The large head of a common sunflower is made up of what?
A cluster of unopened leaves only
A single fruit with no flowers
A sunflower head contains multiple florets rather than a single bloom.
Which part of a sunflower is commonly pressed to produce cooking oil?
Sunflower oil is obtained from seeds, not petals, hairs or roots.
What is the scientific name of the common annual sunflower?
Helianthus annuus is the common sunflower; the alternatives are snowdrop, daffodil and foxglove.
What are the colourful fruits produced by many roses called?
Hips are rose fruits; cones and catkins are different reproductive structures and corms are storage stems.
Rosa is rose; each alternative identifies another flowering genus.
To enjoy a display of rose hips, what should a gardener avoid doing to every flower?
Watering the soil in dry weather
Removing every spent flower prevents hips from developing; ordinary care does not.
Why is opening up the centre of a rose bush one aim of pruning?
To stop all sunlight reaching the leaves
A more open centre improves airflow and can reduce fungal problems.
Dahlias store reserves below ground mainly in which structures?
Dahlias are tuberous-rooted perennials, distinct from true bulbs and corms.
Why are tall, large-flowered dahlias often tied to stakes?
To support their heavy flower-bearing stems
To turn their tubers into bulbs
Support protects top-heavy stems; it does not alter storage organs or prevent growth.
Which conditions threaten dahlia tubers stored over a cold UK winter?
Dahlias are tender; frost-free protection is beneficial rather than the threat.
What gives a bearded iris its 'beard'?
A strip of soft hairs on the lower flower segments
A mass of exposed roots above the flower
Long spines on the leaf tips
A woolly seed coat surrounding each petal
The beard is a line of hairs on the falls; it is not a root or seed structure.
The thick horizontal stems of bearded irises are called what?
The creeping storage stems are rhizomes, not flower parts or seed leaves.
The large red parts of a typical poinsettia display are what?
Poinsettia colour comes from bracts surrounding the much smaller flowers.
Where are a poinsettia's small flowers found?
Among the colourful bracts at the stem tips
On the underside of every green leaf
The small central flowers sit among showy bracts; the alternatives are false locations.
The vivid papery structures around bougainvillea's small flowers are called what?
The coloured papery structures are modified leaves called bracts.
Bougainvilleas originated in South America; the other regions are not their native origin.
Which garden flower is commonly called love-in-a-mist?
Nigella damascena carries this common name; the alternatives are sunflower, rose and tulip.
What creates the 'mist' around a love-in-a-mist flower?
A cloud of steam released by its roots
A coating of white mould on every petal
Mist trapped inside its seed coat
Wispy dissected leaves frame the flowers; no literal mist or mould is involved.
Antirrhinum majus is commonly known as which garden flower?
The RHS profile identifies Antirrhinum majus as snapdragon; alternatives are different genera.
Which common name belongs to plants in the genus Myosotis?
Myosotis is forget-me-not; the three other common names designate different genera.
Which plant bears small, nodding, fragrant white bells above paired broad leaves?
The paired leaves and nodding white bells identify Convallaria majalis among these choices.
A Venus flytrap catches prey using modified versions of which plant part?
The snapping traps are modified leaves rather than floral or underground structures.
Where is the Venus flytrap native?
North and South Carolina in the United States
Its native range is the Carolinas, despite cultivation elsewhere.
What helps trigger a Venus flytrap's trap to snap shut?
Touching sensitive hairs inside the trap
Ripening a fruit beneath the soil
Breaking a root far below the trap
Mechanical stimulation of trigger hairs initiates closure; unrelated events do not.
How do sundews typically catch small insects?
With sticky droplets on their leaves
With thorny fruits that roll downhill
Sundews use sticky leaf glands, not the mechanisms described in the alternatives.
Why is catching prey especially useful to carnivorous plants in nutrient-poor habitats?
It supplies nutrients such as nitrogen
It replaces their entire need for water
It turns their leaves into animal tissue
It allows every species to grow without light
Prey supplements mineral nutrition; carnivory does not remove water or light requirements.
What type of trap is used by a tropical pitcher plant such as Nepenthes?
A pair of wooden jaws beneath the soil
A seed pod that wraps around insects
A moving flower stalk that chases prey
Nepenthes catches prey in modified leaf pitchers; the other mechanisms are invented.
The strong smell of a flowering titan arum is often compared with what?
Titan arum emits a carrion-like odour, not the pleasant scents listed.
Is the titan arum a carnivorous plant?
No; insects visit it as pollinators
Yes; it digests every visiting insect
Only while its leaf is green
Titan arum attracts pollinators with carrion mimicry but does not digest them.
What does the titan arum's huge flowering structure contain?
Many small flowers on a central spike
One enormous flower with a single petal
It is an inflorescence rather than a single giant flower or cone cluster.
Which habitat is natural for the giant waterlily Victoria amazonica?
Freshwater lakes and backwaters of the Amazon basin
Dry sand dunes of the Sahara
Victoria amazonica is a freshwater tropical aquatic plant, not marine or desert.
What distinctive feature occurs around the edge of a giant waterlily's circular leaf?
The large floating leaf has a raised rim; the other options do not describe its margin.
Which insects pollinate Victoria amazonica in the wild?
Beetles are attracted and temporarily trapped by the flower's pollination mechanism.
The genus name Victoria, used for giant waterlilies, honours whom?
The botanical name honours Queen Victoria; the other named people are not the honouree.
What is the sensitive plant, Mimosa pudica, famous for doing when touched?
Mimosa pudica folds its compound leaves in response to touch; none of the alternatives occurs.
How many long-lived foliage leaves does a mature Welwitschia normally produce?
Its two leaves persist and split into strips; apparent many strips are not new leaves.
Welwitschia is associated with which environment?
Welwitschia is a desert gymnosperm of Namibia and Angola, not an aquatic or polar plant.
The monkey puzzle tree is native to parts of which two countries?
Araucaria araucana is native to Chile and Argentina; the other pairs are outside its native range.
Which group of plants includes the monkey puzzle tree?
The monkey puzzle is a seed-cone-bearing evergreen conifer.
What is unusual about where cacao trees produce many of their flowers?
They grow directly from the trunk and older branches
They grow only at the tips of roots
They float free on nearby water
Cacao shows cauliflory, with flowers borne on older woody parts.
Which part of the cacao plant provides the main raw material for chocolate?
Cacao beans are seeds; bark, leaves and petals are not the chocolate raw material.
Which small insects naturally pollinate cacao flowers?
Cacao flowers are adapted to tiny midge pollinators, not the listed larger or nonpollinating insects.
The plant that produces culinary vanilla belongs to which flower family?
Vanilla planifolia is an orchid, despite its climbing habit and edible cured pods.
How does the vanilla plant attach itself to trees as it climbs?
Aerial roots cling to supports; pods and traps are not its climbing organs.
Which part of a vanilla plant is cured to make vanilla pods for flavouring?
Culinary pods are the cured fruits containing tiny seeds.
The part of ginger commonly used in cooking is botanically what?
A true root with no stem tissue
Ginger is harvested for its rhizome, often loosely called ginger root.
Saffron is obtained from which part of the saffron crocus flower?
The spice consists of dried stigmas, not petals, sepals or pollen.
